# **Software Development Plan** 

# 

1. # **Introduction** {#introduction}

   This Software Development Plan describes how the Phy6 team will build the Minimum Viable Product (MVP) of PhysiX between 05 October and 13 December 2026\. It defines what the project delivers and when, how the five team members are organized, how much effort the work is expected to take, how the work is divided into phases, sprints and builds, and how progress, risks and changes are controlled.

   

   The product itself, including its users, features and quality requirements, is described in the PhysiX Vision document, and the behaviour of each feature is described in the PhysiX Use-Case Specification. This plan is reviewed and updated at the end of every sprint.

2. # **Project Overview** {#project-overview}

   1. ## **Project Purpose, Scope, and Objectives** {#project-purpose,-scope,-and-objectives}

   **Purpose:** This project delivers the Minimum Viable Product (MVP) of PhysiX, the first release of the product described in the PhysiX Vision document. The MVP offers the complete PhysiX experience on two experiments: finding an experiment in the library, carrying it out with step-by-step guidance, recording and comparing results, asking the AI lab assistant for help, and exploring apparatus freely in Open Lab. This lets schools and Phy6 validate the product with real users before more experiments and account-based features are added.

**Scope:** The MVP includes the following features of the Vision document:

* Experiment Library (UC02): the full catalogue for Grades 6–12, organized by grade, chapter and lesson; only Simple Pendulum and Ohm’s Law can be started, and all other experiments are marked “Coming soon”.  
* Guided Experiments (UC03): Simple Pendulum (UC03.1) and Ohm’s Law, Grade 11 Lesson 23 (UC03.2), with the parameters, ranges and accuracy stated in Feature 3 of the Vision document.  
* Measurements and Results (UC04): data table, graph and trial comparison for both experiments.  
* AI Lab Assistant (UC05): required in the MVP; both experiments must keep working when the AI service is unavailable.  
* Open Lab (UC06): the apparatus drawer contains the apparatus of the two experiments.  
* The non-functional requirements of the Vision document that apply to these features: Usability (NFR-U1 to NFR-U7), Browser and Platform Compatibility, Performance, Reliability and Robustness, Maintainability, Physics Consistency, and Documentation and Help.  
  The following are planned for later releases and are not part of this project: User Accounts (UC01), Experiment History (UC07), Export Results (UC08), Report a Content Error (UC09), the Security and Privacy and Availability and Capacity requirements that depend on accounts, and all further guided experiments.  
    
  **Roadmap:** After the MVP, PhysiX is planned to grow in the following releases. Each release will have its own plan; no dates are committed in this plan.  
* Release 2 – Accounts and results: user accounts, experiment history, export of results and content error reports (UC01, UC07, UC08, UC09).  
* Release 3 onwards – Curriculum expansion: new guided experiments added chapter by chapter as specializations of UC03. The order is the remaining Grade 11 experiments identified in the textbook inventory first, then Grades 10 and 12, then Natural Science for Grades 6–9. The Open Lab apparatus drawer grows with each new experiment.

**Objectives:** The MVP is accepted when, by 13/Dec/2026:

* both experiments can be completed from the library to the result summary, and their reference tests meet the accuracy stated in the Vision document (pendulum period within 1% of T \= 2π√(l/g); displayed current equal to U/R after rounding);  
* every item of the usability checklist (NFR-U1 to NFR-U7) passes and is signed by the customer representative;  
* the compatibility smoke test passes on all five supported browser and operating-system combinations;  
* the AI lab assistant answers a prepared set of questions for every step of both experiments, and both experiments keep working when the AI service is disconnected;  
* the performance targets of the included features are met on the reference computer;  
* the MVP is deployed at a public web address, with a user guide and a teacher guide.

  2. ## **Assumptions and Constraints** {#assumptions-and-constraints}

	**Assumptions:**

* The five team members can deliver the MVP within the estimated 350 person-hours (Section 4.1) alongside their other courses.  
* The technology comparison carried out in Sprint 2 shows that the planned 3D interactions can run in the browser with Three.js and React Three Fiber. At the end of Sprint 2, the code repository contains only the project setup; feature implementation starts in Sprint 3\.  
* The textbook formulas T \= 2π√(l/g) and I \= U/R are adequate reference models for the two experiments within the ranges stated in the Vision document.  
* An AI service provider with a free usage tier sufficient for development and demonstration is available. The provider is selected in the first week of Sprint 3\.  
* A physics content expert (an experienced physics teacher) is available to review both experiments before Build 3\.  
* Typical school computers are at least as capable as the reference computer defined in Section 5.3 of the Vision document.

**Constraints:**

* **Schedule:** the project has a fixed duration of 10 weeks, divided into five two-week sprints from 05/Oct/2026 to 13/Dec/2026. The milestone dates in Section 2.3 cannot be moved.  
* **Team:** the team is fixed at five members; no members will be added.  
* **Budget:** the cash budget is zero. Only free, open-source or education-tier tools and services are used, and the AI service is used within its free tier. Any expected paid cost is discussed with the customer representative before it is incurred.  
* **Technology (selected in Sprint 2):** React with TypeScript and Vite for the web application; Three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei for the 3D laboratory; the team’s own TypeScript physics solvers, kept independent of the 3D display; the Rapier physics engine only for experiments that need collisions, which the MVP experiments do not; Zustand for application state; Recharts or uPlot for graphs; Tailwind CSS with shadcn/ui for interface components; Vitest and Playwright for automated tests. AI requests pass through a server-side adapter, so that the AI service key is never exposed in the browser. Babylon.js was evaluated and not selected.  
* **Platform:** desktop and laptop browsers listed in Section 5.2 of the Vision document; phones and tablets are not supported.  
* **Scope:** the MVP scope in Section 2.1 is fixed for this project. Any change is handled as a change request (Section 4.3.3).

3. # **Project Organization** {#project-organization}

   1. ## **Organizational Structure** {#organizational-structure}

*![C:\\Users\\G15 5515\\AppData\\Local\\Microsoft\\Windows\\INetCache\\Content.MSO\\8D6509B.tmp][image1]*  
	Phy6 consists of five members. The Project Manager, who is also the Business Analyst, leads the team, plans the sprints and is accountable for every deliverable. The Software Architect owns the technical structure of the application. The other three members own the user interface, the physics models, and the AI and quality assurance work. Each work item in Jira has exactly one owner and one reviewer; work done by the Project Manager is reviewed by another member.

	Two review authorities sit outside the team. The customer representative, a role played in this project by the course instructor and teaching assistants, reviews every milestone deliverable and accepts the MVP. The physics content expert, an experienced physics teacher engaged as an adviser, reviews the procedure, formulas and accuracy of each experiment before it is released.

4. # **Management Process** {#management-process}

   1. ## **Project Estimates** {#project-estimates}

   **Estimation basis:** The estimate covers all project work for the MVP over the fixed 10-week schedule (05/Oct/2026 – 13/Dec/2026): requirements, architecture, implementation, testing, integration, documentation and project management. It is expressed in person-hours and was prepared bottom-up by the team from the work breakdown structure in Section 4.2.1. Because every member also attends other courses, the figures are planning targets and are re-estimated at the end of every sprint.

   

| Team member / role | Primary estimate focus | Effort (person-hours) | Share |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Đặng Trần Tuấn Khôi \- Project Manager / Business Analyst | Sprint planning, Jira, weekly reports and decision log, requirement scope and acceptance criteria, milestone reviews, final presentation | 70 | 20.0% |
| Trần Thiên Phúc \- Software Architect / 3D Developer | Software Architecture Document, project setup and deployment, pendulum and circuit 3D scenes, apparatus interactions, Open Lab, build integration | 70 | 20.0% |
| Võ Quốc Linh \- Backend and AI Developer / QA | Experiment catalogue data, AI lab assistant and server-side adapter, traceability, test plan, system testing, test report | 70 | 20.0% |
| Trần Đặng Lê Huy — UI/UX Designer / Frontend Developer | UI design, Experiment Library, step list, controls, data table, graph and comparison, usability checklist, user guide and teacher guide | 70 | 20.0% |
| Nguyễn Văn Lê Bảo — Physics Developer / Tester | Pendulum and Ohm’s law solvers, reference tests, units, ranges and accuracy, physics validation of readings and graphs | 70 | 20.0% |
| Total | Five members; reviews and shared testing included | 350 | 100% |

**Sprint effort allocation (person-hours):**

| Sprint / dates | Planned effort | Re-estimation checkpoint |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| S1 – 05-18 Oct | 55 | Baseline scope, initial documents and UI sketches, task ownership and first risks. |
| S2 – 19 Oct-01 Nov | 70 | Requirements baseline and technology selection; estimate reviewed at the end of the sprint (see below). |
| S3 – 02-15 Nov | 75 | After Build 1: compare actual and estimated effort for the pendulum and adjust the Ohm’s law and Open Lab estimates. |
| S4 – 16-29 Nov | 80 | After Build 2: re-estimate the remaining testing and defect fixing; protect the MVP scope. |
| S5 – 30 Nov-13 Dec | 70 | Regression testing, defect fixing, documentation and handover only; no new scope. |

**Estimate review at the end of Sprint 2 (01/Nov/2026):** During Sprint 2 the scope changed. Projectile Motion was replaced by Ohm’s Law, the AI lab assistant became mandatory instead of optional, and Open Lab was limited to the apparatus of the two experiments. Ohm’s Law replaces an experiment rather than adding one, and limiting Open Lab reduces its effort, so this plan keeps the total at 350 person-hours. Because the AI lab assistant is now mandatory, its work starts in Sprint 3 instead of being left until the end (Section 4.2.3). The team confirms or adjusts these figures at Sprint 3 planning on 02/Nov/2026. From Sprint 3, actual hours are recorded in Jira for every task and compared with this estimate at every sprint review.

**Budget and tools:** The planned cash budget is zero. The team uses free, open-source or education-tier tools: Jira for task tracking, GitHub for source code and continuous integration, Google Drive for documents, Figma for UI design, a free hosting service with serverless functions for deployment, and the free tier of the selected AI service. No paid service or 3D asset is assumed. If a free-tier limit threatens delivery, the team first chooses a free alternative or reduces non-essential work; any expected cost is discussed with the customer representative before it is incurred.

**Estimation method and control:** At each sprint planning meeting, the team estimates every task of the sprint in ideal hours using planning poker, taking one already-completed task as the reference. At each sprint review, the Project Manager compares estimated and actual hours, completed acceptance criteria and open defects, and records the revised forecast in Jira and the weekly report. The end date cannot move, so if the work falls behind, scope is protected in this order: Guided Experiments and Measurements and Results (UC03, UC03.1, UC03.2, UC04) first, then the AI lab assistant (UC05), then the Experiment Library (UC02), and finally Open Lab interactions (UC06), which are the first to be simplified.

   Every sprint starts on Monday with a planning meeting, at which the team selects tasks from the Jira backlog, estimates them with planning poker, assigns one owner and one reviewer to each task and agrees its acceptance criteria. A short check-in at the end of the first week compares progress with the plan. On the last day of the sprint (Sunday), the sprint review demonstrates the completed work and records open defects, and the retrospective agrees on one or two improvements for the next sprint.

**Work breakdown structure**

1. Project management – 1.1 sprint planning and reviews; 1.2 weekly reports and decision log; 1.3 risk and change management; 1.4 milestone submissions.  
2. Requirements – 2.1 interviews and survey; 2.2 Vision; 2.3 Use-Case Specification; 2.4 textbook experiment inventory; 2.5 UI interaction specification and prototype.  
3. Architecture and design – 3.1 3D technology comparison; 3.2 Software Architecture Document; 3.3 experiment data format and catalogue structure.  
4. Implementation – 4.1 project setup and continuous integration; 4.2 Experiment Library (UC02); 4.3 guided-experiment framework and step list (UC03); 4.4 Simple Pendulum: solver, 3D scene, controls (UC03.1); 4.5 Ohm’s Law: solver, circuit scene, wiring (UC03.2); 4.6 measurements, data table, graph and comparison (UC04); 4.7 AI lab assistant and server-side adapter (UC05); 4.8 Open Lab and apparatus drawer (UC06).  
5. Testing – 5.1 physics reference tests; 5.2 test plan and test cases; 5.3 integration tests; 5.4 system tests (usability, browser compatibility, performance); 5.5 defect fixing; 5.6 test report.  
6. Deployment and handover – 6.1 deployment at a public web address; 6.2 user guide and teacher guide; 6.3 final presentation and demo.

3. ## **Project Monitoring and Control** {#project-monitoring-and-control}

   1. ### *Reporting* {#reporting}

Project status is reported and controlled through the following channels and artifacts:

* **Jira board (updated daily):** every task has one owner, one reviewer, an estimate and a status (To Do → In Progress → In Review → Testing → Done). A task is Done only when the reviewer has accepted it and the evidence (document section, commit, build or screenshot) is linked. Owners post progress as a comment in the format \[PROGRESS yyyy-mm-dd\]: done since last update, remaining work, blockers, evidence, actual and remaining hours, reviewer.  
* **Weekly report (every Sunday):** prepared by the Project Manager on the course template, listing achievements with percentage complete, issues with their impact, owner and action date, and next week’s goals, each linked to its Jira evidence.  
* **Sprint meetings:** planning on the first day of each sprint, a check-in at the end of the first week, and review and retrospective on the last day. Minutes, decisions and actions are stored in the shared Google Drive folder.  
* **Decision log:** every scope or product decision is recorded with its date, the person who decided, the reason and the affected documents.  
* **Risk register:** the risks in Section 4.3.2 are reviewed at every weekly meeting, and the top five are reported in the weekly report.  
* **Quick communication:** Messenger for urgent messages and short discussions; Slack for task reminders and deadline follow-up.  
* **Escalation:** a blocker that is not solved within two days is raised to the Project Manager, who decides on an action at the next meeting or earlier.

  2. ### *Risk Management*  {#risk-management}

  Risks are identified, analysed and prioritized with the method of the course (LN03). Probability is rated Unlikely (10), Seldom (25), Occasional (50), Likely (75) or Frequently (90). Impact (loss) is rated Negligible (10), Insignificant (25), Moderate (50), Serious (75) or Catastrophic (90). Risk exposure is Probability × Impact, and risks are ranked by exposure. The register is reviewed at every weekly meeting and re-assessed at the end of every sprint.

| Risk ID | Risk Description | Probability | Impact | Risk Exposure | Priority | Mitigation Strategy or Contingency Plan |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| R01 | Building the 3D apparatus interactions (dragging the bob, connecting wires, placing apparatus in Open Lab) takes much longer than estimated. | Likely (75) | Serious (75) | 5625 | 1 | Mitigation: build the pendulum interaction first in Week 5 as a spike; use Drei interaction helpers; let wire ends snap to terminals; always offer typed values as an alternative to dragging. Contingency: simplify Open Lab to placing and connecting the apparatus of the two experiments. |
| R02 | Members have less time than planned because of other courses and end-of-semester exams (late November – December). | Likely (75) | Serious (75) | 5625 | 2 | Mitigation: finish all feature work by Build 2 (29 Nov) so that Sprint 5 is testing only; name a backup for each work area; track actual hours weekly. Contingency: move visual polish to Release 2 while keeping every MVP objective. |
| R03 | Requirements or document format change late, as happened in Sprint 2\. | Likely (75) | Moderate (50) | 3750 | 3 | Mitigation: freeze the MVP scope at PA3; handle every change as a change request with its effect on effort and dates (Section 4.3.3); keep traceability between the Vision, use cases and tests so that affected parts are found quickly. |
| R04 | No AI service with a free tier meets the needs for answer quality, speed and cost, or its limits are reached during testing or the demo. | Occasional (50) | Serious (75) | 3750 | 4 | Mitigation: compare at least two providers in Week 5; use an adapter so that the provider can be changed; limit questions to 30 per hour; cache answers to prepared questions. Contingency: answer prepared questions from a reviewed built-in answer set when the service fails. |
| R05 | The AI lab assistant gives incorrect or misleading physics explanations. | Occasional (50) | Serious (75) | 3750 | 5 | Mitigation: send only the current experiment context; restrict answers to the current experiment; quote values only from PhysiX’s instruments; have Bảo and the physics content expert review the answers to the prepared question set; show a warning under every answer and a ‘Report this answer’ link. |
| R06 | The physics solvers, the 3D scene and the interface do not work together correctly (for example, readings differ from the animation). | Occasional (50) | Serious (75) | 3750 | 6 | Mitigation: one shared state store; solver interfaces defined in the SAD before coding; integrate continuously; continuous integration runs all tests on every pull request. |
| R07 | Effort is underestimated because the team has no historical data. | Occasional (50) | Serious (75) | 3750 | 7 | Mitigation: estimate with planning poker; compare estimated and actual hours at every sprint review from Sprint 3; Sprint 5 contains no new features and acts as a buffer. |
| R08 | 3D scenes run too slowly on school computers with integrated graphics. | Occasional (50) | Moderate (50) | 2500 | 8 | Mitigation: low-polygon models, few lights and shadows; measure on the reference computer from Build 1\. Contingency: provide a lower-quality graphics setting. |
| R09 | A supported browser, especially Safari on macOS, shows the 3D scene or graphs incorrectly. | Occasional (50) | Moderate (50) | 2500 | 9 | Mitigation: run the compatibility smoke test on every build, not only in Sprint 5; use only WebGL 2.0 features supported by all listed browsers; arrange access to a Mac before Build 1\. |
| R10 | The physics content expert is not available in time to review the experiments. | Occasional (50) | Moderate (50) | 2500 | 10 | Mitigation: contact the expert in Sprint 3 and agree on review dates before Build 2; Bảo prepares a short review pack. Contingency: ask the physics teachers interviewed in PA0 to review. |
| R11 | Simulated results do not match the textbook because of a formula, unit or rounding error. | Seldom (25) | Serious (75) | 1875 | 11 | Mitigation: solvers independent of the 3D display, with reference tests run in continuous integration; every formula change reviewed by a second member and the physics content expert. |
| R12 | A key member becomes unavailable (for example, through illness) just before a build. | Seldom (25) | Serious (75) | 1875 | 12 | Mitigation: every work area has a backup who reviews its code; documentation and setup instructions are kept in the repository. |
| R13 | Preparing the Grades 6-12 catalogue data (chapters, lessons and experiments) takes longer than planned. | Likely (75) | Insignificant (25) | 1875 | 13 | Mitigation: complete Grade 11 first and list other grades at chapter and lesson level; fill in experiments gradually and mark them “Coming soon”. |
| R14 | Limits of the free hosting service (bandwidth, request limits, slow start-up) affect the demo. | Seldom (25) | Moderate (50) | 1250 | 14 | Mitigation: deploy early, at Build 2; keep 3D assets small. Contingency: run the final demo from a local build. |

     3. ### *Configuration Management* {#configuration-management}

  **Source code:** A GitHub repository stores the application code, physics solvers, tests, 3D assets and technical notes. The main branch is protected. Each Jira task is developed on its own branch named after the task (for example, SCRUM-90-pendulum-solver) and merged through a pull request only after at least one other member has approved it and continuous integration (linting, unit tests and physics reference tests) has passed. Builds are tagged build-1, build-2 and mvp-1.0. Dependency versions are fixed in the committed lock file.

  **Documents:** A shared Google Drive folder stores plans, requirements, designs, reports and meeting minutes, with one subfolder per milestone (PA1–PA5). Files are named Phy6-PhysiX-\<Document\>-v\<version\>, every document keeps its revision history, and a read-only copy of each submitted version is kept. Jira tasks link to the documents and commits they produce.

  **Secrets and third-party assets:** The AI service key is stored only in the server-side environment variables of the hosting service and is never committed to the repository; the repository contains an example file listing only the variable names. The licence of every third-party library and 3D model is recorded in a credits file.

  **Change control:** Anyone may request a change by adding a \[CHANGE yyyy-mm-dd\] comment in Jira, stating the old and new requirement, the reason, who requested it, the affected documents and tasks, and the expected effect on effort and dates. The Project Manager assesses the request with the owners of the affected work. An approved change is applied to every affected document (Vision, Use-Case Specification, SDP), with a new revision history entry, and is reported in the weekly report. A rejected change is recorded together with the reason.
